**Omladinski fudbalski klub Grbalj** ([Serbian Cyrillic](/wiki/Serbian_Cyrillic_alphabet "Serbian Cyrillic alphabet"): Омладински фудбалски клуб Грбаљ, Serbo-Croatian pronunciation: [[gr̩̂baʎ]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian "Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian")) is a [Montenegrin](/wiki/Montenegro "Montenegro") professional [football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") club based in the small town of [Radanovići](/wiki/Radanovi%C4%87i,_Kotor "Radanovići, Kotor"), municipality of [Kotor](/wiki/Kotor "Kotor"). They currently compete in the [Montenegrin Second League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Second_League "Montenegrin Second League").

History
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=OFK_Grbalj&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The first football club in Radanovići, which existed only few seasons, was founded in 1970. After many years, the club was refounded in June 1995[[1]](#cite_note-1) and in their first season the team gained promotion to the [Montenegrin Republic League](/wiki/Montenegrin_clubs_in_Yugoslav_football_competitions_(1946%E2%80%932006)#Montenegrin_Republic_League "Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946–2006)") for the 1996–97 season (third tier of the [FR Yugoslavia](/wiki/FR_Yugoslavia "FR Yugoslavia") football system). After only three seasons in the Republic League, in the summer of 1999, OFK Grbalj (*OFC Humpback*) became a member of the [FR Yugoslavia Second League](/wiki/1999%E2%80%932000_Second_League_of_FR_Yugoslavia "1999–2000 Second League of FR Yugoslavia"), which was the biggest success of the team until 2006.[[2]](#cite_note-2) OFK Grbalj spent four seasons in the Second Yugoslav League.  
After [Montenegrin independence](/wiki/Montenegrin_independence_referendum,_2006 "Montenegrin independence referendum, 2006"), OFK Grbalj became a member of the [Montenegrin First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"). In the 2006–07 season, the team achieved third place, just behind two of the most successful teams in national competitions, [Zeta](/wiki/FK_Zeta "FK Zeta") and [Budućnost Podgorica](/wiki/FK_Budu%C4%87nost_Podgorica "FK Budućnost Podgorica"). Over the next two seasons, OFK Grbalj finished as a fourth-placed team. During subsequent seasons, the team didn't achieve the same successes as in their first seasons in top-tier competition, but they were never relegated from the First League.  
OFK Grbalj holds two all-time records in the Montenegrin First League. On 29 May 2010 they defeated [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom "FK Kom") 11–0, which is the biggest margin of victory in the history of league. Five years later, on 23 May 2015, OFK Grbalj beat [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") in [Bar](/wiki/Bar,_Montenegro "Bar, Montenegro") 7–0, which is the biggest away victory in league.  
In the 2016–17 season, OFK Grbalj had the greatest success in their history by reaching the [Montenegrin Cup final](/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Montenegrin_Cup "2016–17 Montenegrin Cup"). They lost game against [Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Sutjeska Nikšić") 1–0.  
After 14 consecutive seasons in top-tier, OFK Grbalj finished as a last-placed team in [2019-20 Montenegrin First League](/wiki/2019-20_Montenegrin_First_League "2019-20 Montenegrin First League"). After the campaign full of disappointing results, team from Radanovići was relegated to [Montenegrin Second League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Second_League "Montenegrin Second League").

Stadium
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=OFK_Grbalj&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Stadium")]

Main article: [Stadion Donja Sutvara](/wiki/Stadion_Donja_Sutvara "Stadion Donja Sutvara")

OFK Grbalj play at [Stadion Donja Sutvara](/wiki/Stadion_Donja_Sutvara "Stadion Donja Sutvara"), near the main road between [Budva](/wiki/Budva "Budva") and [Kotor](/wiki/Kotor "Kotor"). Stadium capacity is 1,500 seats on one stand and it doesn't meet UEFA standards for European competitions. Except the main ground, there is a smaller artificial pitch at Donja Sutvara football complex.

**Alexandre Boucaut** (born 10 August 1980) is a [Belgian](/wiki/Belgian_people "Belgian people") football referee. He made his debut in the [Belgian Pro League](/wiki/Belgian_Pro_League "Belgian Pro League") at 8 February 2009 in a game between [KVC Westerlo](/wiki/KVC_Westerlo "KVC Westerlo") and [KSC Lokeren](/wiki/KSC_Lokeren "KSC Lokeren"). As profession, he's head of a bank in [Ath](/wiki/Ath "Ath").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

The **Belgian Pro League**,[[1]](#cite_note-1) officially the **[Jupiler](/wiki/Jupiler "Jupiler") Pro League** (Dutch pronunciation: [[ˈʑypilɛr ˈproː ˌlik]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Dutch "Help:IPA/Dutch")) for sponsorship reasons, is a professional [association football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") league in [Belgium](/wiki/Belgium "Belgium") and the highest level of the [Belgian football league system](/wiki/Belgian_football_league_system "Belgian football league system"). Contested by 16 clubs from the [2023–24 season](/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_Belgian_Pro_League "2023–24 Belgian Pro League") until 2025–26 when it will expand to 18 teams from 2026–27 onwards, it operates on a system of [promotion and relegation](/wiki/Promotion_and_relegation "Promotion and relegation") with the [Challenger Pro League](/wiki/Challenger_Pro_League "Challenger Pro League").

Seasons run from late July to late March, with teams playing 30 matches each in the regular season, and then entering **Play-offs I** (also known as the *Championship Playoff*, *title playoffs* or *Champions' play-offs*[[2]](#cite_note-Officialranking-2)), **Play-offs II** (also known as the *Europa League playoff* or *Europe play-offs*[[2]](#cite_note-Officialranking-2)) or **Play-offs III** (also known as the *Relegation play-offs*[[2]](#cite_note-Officialranking-2)) according to their position in the regular season. Play-offs I are contested by the top-six clubs in the regular season, with each club playing each other twice. The teams finishing in 15th and 16th place are relegated directly, however, the 14th place team plays a promotion-relegation play-off against the 3rd place team of the Challenger Pro League.

The competition was created in 1895 by the [Royal Belgian Football Association](/wiki/Royal_Belgian_Football_Association "Royal Belgian Football Association") and was first won by [FC Liégeois](/wiki/RFC_Li%C3%A8ge "RFC Liège"). Of the 78 clubs to have competed in the first division since its creation, 16 have been crowned champions of Belgium. [Anderlecht](/wiki/R.S.C._Anderlecht "R.S.C. Anderlecht") is the most successful league club with 34 titles, followed by [Club Brugge](/wiki/Club_Brugge_KV "Club Brugge KV") (19), [Union Saint-Gilloise](/wiki/Royale_Union_Saint-Gilloise "Royale Union Saint-Gilloise") (12) and [Standard Liège](/wiki/Standard_Li%C3%A8ge "Standard Liège") (10). It is currently ranked 8th in the [UEFA rankings](/wiki/UEFA_coefficient "UEFA coefficient") of leagues based on performances in European competitions over the last five-years.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The competition was ranked 3rd when the UEFA first published their ranking in 1979 and also the next year in 1980, which is the best ranking the Belgian First Division has ever achieved.

History
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Origins (1895–1914)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origins (1895–1914)")]

The first league in Belgian football was held in [1895–96](/wiki/1895%E2%80%9396_Belgian_First_Division "1895–96 Belgian First Division") as a [round-robin tournament](/wiki/Round-robin_tournament "Round-robin tournament") with seven teams: [Antwerp FC](/wiki/Royal_Antwerp_F.C. "Royal Antwerp F.C."), [FC Brugeois](/wiki/Club_Brugge "Club Brugge"), [FC Liégeois](/wiki/RFC_Li%C3%A8ge "RFC Liège"), [RC de Bruxelles](/wiki/K.F.C._Rhodienne-De_Hoek "K.F.C. Rhodienne-De Hoek"), [Léopold Club de Bruxelles](/wiki/R._L%C3%A9opold_Uccle_Forestoise "R. Léopold Uccle Forestoise"), [SC de Bruxelles](/wiki/S.C._de_Bruxelles "S.C. de Bruxelles"), and [Union d'Ixelles](/wiki/Union_F.C._d%27Ixelles "Union F.C. d'Ixelles"). FC Liégeois became the first champion of Belgium. The first eight titles in Belgian football were all won by FC Liégeois or RC de Bruxelles. There was no promotion and relegation system at the time, but the last two finishers (FC Brugeois and Union d'Ixelles) withdrew and a new club entered the competition ([Athletic and Running Club de Bruxelles](/wiki/Athletic_and_Running_Club_de_Bruxelles "Athletic and Running Club de Bruxelles")). During the [1896–97](/wiki/1896%E2%80%9397_Belgian_First_Division "1896–97 Belgian First Division") season, SC de Bruxelles withdrew, so the [1897–98](/wiki/1897%E2%80%9398_Belgian_First_Division "1897–98 Belgian First Division") season was played by five clubs. In the seasons [1898–99](/wiki/1898%E2%80%9399_Belgian_First_Division "1898–99 Belgian First Division") and [1899–1900](/wiki/1899%E2%80%931900_Belgian_First_Division "1899–1900 Belgian First Division"), the football association introduced a new format with two leagues at the top level and a final game in two legs. The format changed back to one league with nine clubs in [1900–01](/wiki/1900%E2%80%9301_Belgian_First_Division "1900–01 Belgian First Division"), then again to two leagues from [1901–02](/wiki/1901%E2%80%9302_Belgian_First_Division "1901–02 Belgian First Division") to [1903–04](/wiki/1903%E2%80%9304_Belgian_First_Division "1903–04 Belgian First Division"), this time with a final round among the top two teams of each league. In [1904–05](/wiki/1904%E2%80%9305_Belgian_First_Division "1904–05 Belgian First Division"), the championship was organised with one league of 11 teams. Athletic and Running Club de Bruxelles withdrew during the season and, from the [1906 season](/wiki/1905%E2%80%9306_Belgian_First_Division "1905–06 Belgian First Division") on, a system of promotion and relegation was introduced with the winner of the second division replacing the last-placed team of the first division. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In [1906–07](/wiki/1906%E2%80%9307_Belgian_First_Division "1906–07 Belgian First Division"), [Union Saint-Gilloise](/wiki/Royale_Union_Saint-Gilloise "Royale Union Saint-Gilloise") won their fourth consecutive title as RC de Bruxelles had from 1899–1900 to 1902–03. Both clubs claimed the next three titles before [CS Brugeois](/wiki/Cercle_Brugge_K.S.V. "Cercle Brugge K.S.V.") won their first title, finishing one point ahead their rival of FC Brugeois. At the end of the 1907–08 season, the number of teams in the first division was increased from 10 to 12 clubs, with Promotion champion [RC de Gand](/wiki/K.R.C._Gent-Zeehaven "K.R.C. Gent-Zeehaven") and runner-up [ESC Forest](/wiki/R.E._Sport%27s_Club "R.E. Sport's Club") being promoted while no first division was relegated. As [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") approached, Daring Club de Bruxelles confirmed its status of challenger, even winning the title in [1911–12](/wiki/1911%E2%80%9312_Belgian_First_Division "1911–12 Belgian First Division") and [1913–14](/wiki/1913%E2%80%9314_Belgian_First_Division "1913–14 Belgian First Division"). Only Union Saint-Gilloise could face them in that period, winning the [1912–13](/wiki/1912%E2%80%9313_Belgian_First_Division "1912–13 Belgian First Division") championship with a better goal difference. Since 1911–12, two clubs are relegated each year to the Promotion and two clubs from the Promotion are promoted.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

### After World War I (1919–1945)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: After World War I (1919–1945)")]

During World War I, the football championship was suspended. It resumed in [1919–20](/wiki/1919%E2%80%9320_Belgian_First_Division "1919–20 Belgian First Division") with FC Brugeois claiming their first title after five second places, among which were two lost final games and one lost test-match. At the end of the [1920–21 season](/wiki/1920%E2%80%9321_Belgian_First_Division "1920–21 Belgian First Division"), the number of teams was increased from 12 to 14, with only [Uccle Sport](/wiki/R._Uccle_Sport "R. Uccle Sport"), the last-placed team of the first division, being relegated, and the first three teams from the Promotion being promoted ([Standard Club Liégeois](/wiki/Standard_Li%C3%A8ge "Standard Liège"), [FC Malinois](/wiki/KV_Mechelen "KV Mechelen"), and [RSC Anderlechtois](/wiki/R.S.C._Anderlecht "R.S.C. Anderlecht")). From [1921–22](/wiki/1921%E2%80%9322_Belgian_First_Division "1921–22 Belgian First Division") to [1931–32](/wiki/1931%E2%80%9332_Belgian_First_Division "1931–32 Belgian First Division"), the decade was dominated by teams from the province of [Antwerp](/wiki/Antwerp_(province) "Antwerp (province)"): [Beerschot AC](/wiki/Beerschot_AC "Beerschot AC"), with [Raymond Braine](/wiki/Raymond_Braine "Raymond Braine"), won their first five titles, Antwerp FC their first two and the small club of [Liersche SK](/wiki/Lierse_S.K._(1906) "Lierse S.K. (1906)") (led by striker [Bernard Voorhoof](/wiki/Bernard_Voorhoof "Bernard Voorhoof")) won their first one in 1931–32. The challengers at the time were CS Brugeois (two titles in that period), Union Saint-Gilloise (one title), Daring Club de Bruxelles and Standard Club Liégeois. Starting 25 December 1932, Union Saint-Gilloise had a record 60 games unbeaten run in the championship (spanning three seasons), winning the [1932–33](/wiki/1932%E2%80%9333_Belgian_First_Division "1932–33 Belgian First Division"), [1933–34](/wiki/1933%E2%80%9334_Belgian_First_Division "1933–34 Belgian First Division"), and [1934–35](/wiki/1934%E2%80%9335_Belgian_First_Division "1934–35 Belgian First Division") titles. The rival of Union during this period was [Daring Club de Bruxelles](/wiki/Daring_Club_de_Bruxelles "Daring Club de Bruxelles"). They claimed the next two championships. Following the come-back of player [Raymond Braine](/wiki/Raymond_Braine "Raymond Braine") to Beerschot, the [Antwerp](/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp") club won the last two titles before [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

On 10 May 1940, German troops invaded Belgium and the seasons 1939–40 and 1940–41 were suspended. The competition resumed in September 1941 and Liersche SK won their second title. At the end of the season, no club was relegated and the number of clubs was increased from 14 to 16. The [next season](/wiki/1942%E2%80%9343_Belgian_First_Division "1942–43 Belgian First Division"), Liersche SK lost three key players (two of them in a bomb attack and the other one due to a heavy injury sustained on the pitch) and they ended at 3rd place while the neighbours of [KV Mechelen](/wiki/KV_Mechelen "KV Mechelen") became champion for the first time in their history. In [1943–44](/wiki/1943%E2%80%9344_Belgian_First_Division "1943–44 Belgian First Division"), Antwerp FC won the title. The league was suspended again in 1944–45 because of World War II.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

### After World War II (1945–1980)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: After World War II (1945–1980)")]

The league resumed play in [1945–46](/wiki/1945%E2%80%9346_Belgian_First_Division "1945–46 Belgian First Division") with a title for KV Mechelen. At the start of that season, the First Division went from 16 to 19 clubs, with three clubs promoted from the First Division and no team being relegated. The [top scorer](/wiki/Belgian_First_Division_top_scorers "Belgian First Division top scorers") award was also introduced that season, won by [Bert De Cleyn](/wiki/Bert_De_Cleyn "Bert De Cleyn") from KV Mechelen. Two seasons later, five clubs were relegated and two promoted. In [1946–47](/wiki/1946%E2%80%9347_Belgian_First_Division "1946–47 Belgian First Division"), RSC Anderlechtois won their first championship with [Jef Mermans](/wiki/Joseph_Mermans "Joseph Mermans") as the key striker and they dominated the Belgian football over the next 9 years with 6 more titles, with KV Mechelen (in [1947–48](/wiki/1947%E2%80%9348_Belgian_First_Division "1947–48 Belgian First Division")) and FC Liégeois (in [1951–52](/wiki/1951%E2%80%9352_Belgian_First_Division "1951–52 Belgian First Division") and [1952–53](/wiki/1952%E2%80%9353_Belgian_First_Division "1952–53 Belgian First Division")) claiming the remaining titles. The [Belgian Golden Shoe](/wiki/Belgian_Golden_Shoe "Belgian Golden Shoe") award was introduced in 1954, rewarding the best player in the first division for the past calendar year, thus over two half seasons. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In the late 1950s Standard lifted the trophy for the first time in [1957–58](/wiki/1957%E2%80%9358_Belgian_First_Division "1957–58 Belgian First Division") and they eventually became one of Anderlecht's biggest rivals in the league (until their 8th title in [1982–83](/wiki/1982%E2%80%9383_Belgian_First_Division "1982–83 Belgian First Division")). The other titles in the late 1950s were won by Antwerp FC and Anderlecht. In the 1960s, the Anderlecht team of [Paul Van Himst](/wiki/Paul_Van_Himst "Paul Van Himst") claimed six titles (with the Belgian record of five consecutives titles between [1963–64](/wiki/1963%E2%80%9364_Belgian_First_Division "1963–64 Belgian First Division") and [1967–68](/wiki/1967%E2%80%9368_Belgian_First_Division "1967–68 Belgian First Division")), while Standard claimed three and Lierse one. Standard, with key player [Wilfried Van Moer](/wiki/Wilfried_Van_Moer "Wilfried Van Moer"), won the first two titles of the 1970s, which gave them their only treble so far (together with the [1968–69](/wiki/1968%E2%80%9369_Belgian_First_Division "1968–69 Belgian First Division") title). [1974–75](/wiki/1974%E2%80%9375_Belgian_First_Division "1974–75 Belgian First Division") was the only season with as many as 20 clubs in the league's history. Belgian clubs started to perform well in European Cups in the 1970s, with Anderlecht winning the [1975–76 European Cup Winners' Cup](/wiki/1975%E2%80%9376_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup "1975–76 European Cup Winners' Cup") and Club Brugge losing to [Liverpool F.C.](/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.") in the [1975–76 UEFA Cup](/wiki/1975%E2%80%9376_UEFA_Cup "1975–76 UEFA Cup") [final](/wiki/1976_UEFA_Cup_Final "1976 UEFA Cup Final"). The following season, Anderlecht lost to [Hamburger SV](/wiki/Hamburger_SV "Hamburger SV") in the [Cup Winners' Cup](/wiki/1976%E2%80%9377_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup "1976–77 European Cup Winners' Cup") final and in [1977–78](/wiki/1977%E2%80%9378_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup "1977–78 European Cup Winners' Cup") won for the second time, while Club Brugge lost the [European Cup](/wiki/1977%E2%80%9378_European_Cup "1977–78 European Cup") to Liverpool F.C.. In the Belgian First Division, Club Brugge claimed four titles in the decade, while Anderlecht claimed two and [R White Daring Molenbeek](/wiki/R.W.D._Molenbeek_(1909) "R.W.D. Molenbeek (1909)") (the successor of Daring Club de Bruxelles) with [Johan Boskamp](/wiki/Johan_Boskamp "Johan Boskamp") and [KSK Beveren](/wiki/K.S.K._Beveren "K.S.K. Beveren") with goalkeeper [Jean-Marie Pfaff](/wiki/Jean-Marie_Pfaff "Jean-Marie Pfaff") each claimed their first Belgian championship. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Recent years (1980–present)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recent years (1980–present)")]

In the 1980s, the European successes continued for Belgian clubs with Standard reaching the [1981–82 European Cup Winners' Cup](/wiki/1981%E2%80%9382_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup "1981–82 European Cup Winners' Cup") final, Anderlecht winning the [1982–83 UEFA Cup](/wiki/1982%E2%80%9383_UEFA_Cup "1982–83 UEFA Cup") and losing the [next UEFA Cup](/wiki/1983%E2%80%9384_UEFA_Cup "1983–84 UEFA Cup") final and KV Mechelen winning the [1987–88 European Cup Winners' Cup](/wiki/1987%E2%80%9388_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup "1987–88 European Cup Winners' Cup"). In the domestic league, Anderlecht won their 20th title in [1986–87](/wiki/1986%E2%80%9387_Belgian_First_Division "1986–87 Belgian First Division"), which was also the 4th of the decade. Club Brugge and Standard each won two titles in the 1980s and KSK Beveren and KV Mechelen one each. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In the 1990s, Belgium's teams performances were diminished in European competitions, with only RSC Anderlecht and Royal Antwerp FC reaching the [European Cup Winners' Cup](/wiki/European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup "European Cup Winners' Cup") final, respectively in [1989–90](/wiki/1989%E2%80%9390_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup "1989–90 European Cup Winners' Cup") and in [1992–93](/wiki/1992%E2%80%9393_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup "1992–93 European Cup Winners' Cup"). In the home league, RSC Anderlecht took four titles during the decade, while Club Brugge cemented their status as main contender with four titles. The remaining two titles went to Lierse SK and newcomer [Racing Genk](/wiki/K.R.C._Genk "K.R.C. Genk"). The 2000s brought a bright European start, with Anderlecht reaching the second group stage in the [2000–01 UEFA Champions League](/wiki/2000%E2%80%9301_UEFA_Champions_League "2000–01 UEFA Champions League"), but the rest of the decade Belgian clubs were again not very successful in European competitions. In the league, RSC Anderlecht won five titles in the decade, with Club Brugge claiming two titles and Racing Genk taking their second title. At the end of the decade, [Standard Liège](/wiki/Standard_Li%C3%A8ge "Standard Liège") returned as a title contender with two consecutive titles, 25 years after their [1982–83](/wiki/1982%E2%80%9383_Belgian_First_Division "1982–83 Belgian First Division") title. At the end of the 2000s, the highest level in Belgian football was reshaped, with a play-off round after the regular season. RSC Anderlecht won the [first championship in this new format](/wiki/Belgian_Pro_League_2009-10 "Belgian Pro League 2009-10"), which was their 30th title. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] After another two titles for Anderlecht, [KAA Gent](/wiki/KAA_Gent "KAA Gent") was the surprise winner of the Championship in 2015. The following seven years, Club Brugge would win the league five times. Anderlecht and Genk won the title on the other occasions. [Union Saint-Gilloise](/wiki/Royale_Union_Saint-Gilloise "Royale Union Saint-Gilloise") came close to shocking the footballing world by almost winning the league in [2021–22](/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Belgian_First_Division_A "2021–22 Belgian First Division A"). In their first season at the top flight in 48 years, they started the play-offs in first place, but came just short of denying Club Brugge their third consecutive title.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Competition format and naming
-----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Competition format and naming")]

The competition format has undergone several changes since 2009, but the most significant one was the introduction of playoffs after completion of the regular season from the 2009–10 season. At that time the number of teams also decreased from 18 to 16 and there was the introduction of matches being played during the [Christmas holidays](/wiki/Christmas "Christmas"). The change was initially met with criticism, with many at that time pointing out that the Dutch [Eredivisie](/wiki/Eredivisie "Eredivisie") has already abandoned playoffs after three seasons. Anderlecht won the first championship in this new format, the [Belgian Pro League 2009-10](/wiki/Belgian_Pro_League_2009-10 "Belgian Pro League 2009-10"), which was their 30th Belgian championship.

Following the 2015–16 season, the number of professional teams in Belgium was brought down to 24, which mostly affected the teams playing at the second level of the Belgian football pyramid as the [Belgian Second Division](/wiki/Belgian_Second_Division "Belgian Second Division") was replaced by the [Belgian First Division B](/wiki/Belgian_First_Division_B "Belgian First Division B") and the number of teams dropped to eight.

Due to the redesign of the UEFA competitions and the extra burden on the football season calendar (4 extra matchdays for clubs in Europe), there was a need to reduce the number of matches in the Belgian League. Despite the playoff format being very successful with added excitement and decisions often at the very end of the season, the clubs could not agree on a format with fewer teams or altered playoffs and hence it was decided end of February 2025 to return to a system without playoffs from the 2026–27 season onwards, while expanding the top division from 16 to 18 teams.

Matches are usually played on Saturdays at 20.00; however, some matchdays are played on Wednesdays. Furthermore, in recent years, some games are played on Fridays or during the weekend at different times (e.g., Saturday at 18.00 or Sunday at 13.00 or 20.00), as decided by the owner of television rights. Each team playing the Pro League must have been granted the Belgian professional football license guaranteeing the club has no excessive debts, has a secure stadium, etc. This was introduced in the 2001–02 season to decrease the number of teams in the division and ensure a higher level of professionalism in the clubs playing in the top flight of Belgian football. Originally, clubs that could not get the license were supposed not to be replaced (and sent to the [third division](/wiki/Belgian_Third_Division "Belgian Third Division")). However, it is still not effective as, for example, [KSK Beveren](/wiki/K.S.K._Beveren "K.S.K. Beveren") finished 18th (last) in 2001–2002, but was saved as [KSC Eendracht Aalst](/wiki/K.S.C._Eendracht_Aalst "K.S.C. Eendracht Aalst") (17th) and [RWD Molenbeek](/wiki/R.W.D._Molenbeek_(1909) "R.W.D. Molenbeek (1909)") (10th) were refused their license.

### Regular season

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Regular season")]

Each of the 16 competitors in the Pro League plays every other team twice in the regular season, for a total of 30 matches between August and April. A win earns three points and a draw earns one point. Teams are ranked by total points, then by total wins and finally by goal difference, number of scored goals, number of away goals, and number of away wins. If teams are still level, a test-match is played in two legs to determine the final order in the standings. A playoff phase is then played from May.

### Championship Play-off

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Championship Play-off")]

The point system in the championship playoff is the same as during the regular season, except that each team starts with half of the points they won in the regular season, rounded up to the nearest integer. The points gained by rounding are deducted in the case of a tie.

The top six teams from the regular season enter the championship playoff, with the first-placed team winning the championship of Belgium. Each team plays their opponents twice and the teams are ranked by points, points from rounding, wins, etc. as in the regular season.

### Europa League Playoff

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Europa League Playoff")]

Until 2016, the teams ranked 7 to 14 after the regular season enter the playoffs 2, with teams ranked 7th, 9th, 12th, and 14th entering group A and teams ranked 8th, 10th, 11th, and 13th entering group B. In each group, each team plays each of its three opponents twice. The winner of each group played the final game in two legs to determine the winner of the playoffs 2. The winner of the playoffs 2 then plays a home and away game against either the fourth-place or fifth-place team from the playoffs 1 for the final Europa League ticket, with the opponent depending on whether the Belgian Cup winner ended in the top four of the playoff 1 or not.

From 2016, the system was changed as now the teams ranked 7 to 16 are joined by six teams from the [Belgian First Division B](/wiki/Belgian_First_Division_B "Belgian First Division B") and divided into four groups of four teams. The winners of each groups now play a single match to determine the overall playoff winner, with the winner playing the fifth-placed team from playoff 1 in a single match for the final Europa League ticket.

### Relegation playoff

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Relegation playoff")]

Until 2015, a relegation playoff was played between the teams ranked 15th and 16th after the regular season. It consisted of five games between the two teams. The 15th-placed team started the playoffs with three points whereas the 16th-placed team started from zero. The loser of the relegation playoff was relegated to the second division. The winner of that playoff had to enter the [Belgian Second Division final round](/wiki/Belgian_Second_Division_final_round "Belgian Second Division final round") with three teams from the second division. The winner of this Final Round played in the First Division the season thereafter.

From 2015 to 2023, the relegation playoff ceased to exist, as now the 16th-place team relegates directly, whereas the 15th placed team takes part in the Europa League playoff. The [2015–16 Belgian Pro League](/wiki/2015%E2%80%9316_Belgian_Pro_League "2015–16 Belgian Pro League") was an exception as during that season the 15th placed team did not take part in any playoff, with the season for that team ending after the regular season.

From 2023 onwards, the relegation play-off was played between the teams ranked 13th and 16th after the regular season. After the relegation play-off battle, two teams are relegated directly to the Challenger Pro League and one team will play against 3rd place of Challenger Pro League due to avoid relegation.

### Qualification for European competitions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Qualification for European competitions")]

For the 2010–11 season, the Belgian champion and the runner-up qualify for the 3rd [UEFA Champions League](/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League "UEFA Champions League") qualifying round (of 4).[[7]](#cite_note-7) The [Belgian Cup](/wiki/Belgian_Cup "Belgian Cup") winner (or the Cup finalist if the Cup winner finished first or second in the league) qualifies for the play-off of the [UEFA Europa League](/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League "UEFA Europa League"). The third-placed team (or the fourth-placed team if the Cup winner finished third in the league) qualifies for the 3rd and last qualifying round and the winner of the game between the play-offs 2 winner and the fourth-placed team (or the fifth-placed team if the Cup winner finished fourth) qualifies for the 2nd qualifying round.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

### Naming

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Naming")]

* 1895–1904: Championship Cup
* 1904–1926: First Division
* 1926–1952: Division of Honour
* 1952–2016: First Division
* 2016–2022: First Division A
* 2022–present: Belgian Pro League

Media coverage
--------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Media coverage")]

The Belgian Football Association sells the television rights for the Belgian First Division every three years. In 2005, the newly created Belgian TV channel [Proximus TV](/wiki/Proximus_TV "Proximus TV") bought the TV rights for a record amount of €36 million per season until 2019–20.

In May 2008, the rights were again sold to Belgacom TV in association with both public broadcasters [VRT](/wiki/Vlaamse_Radio-_en_Televisieomroep "Vlaamse Radio- en Televisieomroep") (Dutch) and [RTBF](/wiki/RTBF "RTBF") (French) for an amount of €45.7 million per season.[[9]](#cite_note-9) RTBF and VRT thus received the rights to show summaries of first division games, as well as rights to a weekly magazine on the competition. Belgacom TV received the rights to show each game in the competition.

On 12 June 2020 Aser's [Eleven Sports](/wiki/Eleven_Sports "Eleven Sports") and the Pro League reached an agreement on the new domestic and international media contract for the coming five years. As exclusive global rights holder, Eleven Sports will air the rights of all Pro League competitions for the next five seasons from 2020–21 until 2024–25, with both public broadcasters Play 4 (Dutch) and RTBF (French) lands the rights for highlights again.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Players
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Players")]

See also: [Belgian Golden Shoe](/wiki/Belgian_Golden_Shoe "Belgian Golden Shoe"), [Belgian professional football awards](/wiki/Belgian_professional_football_awards "Belgian professional football awards"), and [Ebony Shoe](/wiki/Ebony_Shoe "Ebony Shoe")

Players in the Belgian First Division can be of any nationality and a club can sign as many foreign players as desired. The first club to start a game with 11 foreign players was [KSC Lokeren](/wiki/K.S.C._Lokeren_Oost-Vlaanderen "K.S.C. Lokeren Oost-Vlaanderen") in 2001. Every year, players are elected for [Belgian Golden Shoe](/wiki/Belgian_Golden_Shoe "Belgian Golden Shoe") awards, the highest awards a player can receive in Belgian competitions, but also for [Belgian professional football awards](/wiki/Belgian_professional_football_awards "Belgian professional football awards"). Players with African descent, origin or nationality can claim a [Belgian Ebony Shoe](/wiki/Belgian_Ebony_Shoe "Belgian Ebony Shoe") award. Players compete also every season for the Belgian First Division top scorer, since the 1945–46 season.

Main article: [Belgian First Division A top scorers](/wiki/Belgian_First_Division_A_top_scorers "Belgian First Division A top scorers")

[Erwin Vandenbergh](/wiki/Erwin_Vandenbergh "Erwin Vandenbergh") is the only player to have claimed the top scorer title four consecutive times, between 1979–80 and 1982–83 (the first three times while at [Lierse SK](/wiki/Lierse_S.K._(1906) "Lierse S.K. (1906)") and the last time while at [RSC Anderlecht](/wiki/R.S.C._Anderlecht "R.S.C. Anderlecht")). He is also the player to have claimed the most Belgian First Division top scorer titles in his career (six times with three different clubs: three times with Lierse SK, twice with RSC Anderlecht and once with [KAA Gent](/wiki/K.A.A._Gent "K.A.A. Gent")). [Victor Wegria](/wiki/Victor_Wegria "Victor Wegria") and [Josip Weber](/wiki/Josip_Weber "Josip Weber") won the title three consecutive times (resp. between 1958–59 and 1960–61 while at [RFC Liégeois](/wiki/RFC_Li%C3%A8ge "RFC Liège") and between 1991–92 and 1993–94 while at [Cercle Brugge KSV](/wiki/Cercle_Brugge_K.S.V. "Cercle Brugge K.S.V.")). Wegria eventually finished top scorer a 4th time in 1962–63 still with RFC Liégeois, making him the second player with the most top scorer titles in the history of Belgian First Division top scorers.

The introduction of this title of honour in 1945 was maybe a little too late for first winner [Albert De Cleyn](/wiki/Albert_De_Cleyn "Albert De Cleyn") as this player has scored the most goals in the history of the Belgian First Division since 1895 (350 goals in 395 games between 1932 and 1954 with [KV Mechelen](/wiki/Y.R._K.V._Mechelen "Y.R. K.V. Mechelen")), though he won the top scorer title only once. Other players in the top ten of the all-time top scorer ranking in the Belgian First Division include [Joseph Mermans](/wiki/Joseph_Mermans "Joseph Mermans") (three times top scorer, 339 goals overall in 382 games with RSC Anderlecht), [Bernard Voorhoof](/wiki/Bernard_Voorhoof "Bernard Voorhoof") ([Belgium national football team](/wiki/Belgium_national_football_team "Belgium national football team") top scorer, 281 goals in 473 matches with Lierse SK), [Rik Coppens](/wiki/Rik_Coppens "Rik Coppens") (three times top scorer), Erwin Vandenbergh and [Paul Van Himst](/wiki/Paul_Van_Himst "Paul Van Himst") (Belgium top scorer with Bernard Voorhoof, three times top scorer).

The first foreign player to claim the title was Dutchman [Jan Mulder](/wiki/Jan_Mulder_(footballer) "Jan Mulder (footballer)") in 1966–67 with RSC Anderlecht. Since then, 25 foreign players have finished top scorer. Only three foreign players claimed the trophy more than once: [Josip Weber](/wiki/Josip_Weber "Josip Weber") (twice as a Croat and once as a Belgian), Austrian [Alfred Riedl](/wiki/Alfred_Riedl "Alfred Riedl") and most recently Frenchman [Jérémy Perbet](/wiki/J%C3%A9r%C3%A9my_Perbet "Jérémy Perbet").

**Omladinski fudbalski klub Grbalj** ([Serbian Cyrillic](/wiki/Serbian_Cyrillic_alphabet "Serbian Cyrillic alphabet"): Омладински фудбалски клуб Грбаљ, Serbo-Croatian pronunciation: [[gr̩̂baʎ]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian "Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian")) is a [Montenegrin](/wiki/Montenegro "Montenegro") professional [football](/wiki/Association_football "Association football") club based in the small town of [Radanovići](/wiki/Radanovi%C4%87i,_Kotor "Radanovići, Kotor"), municipality of [Kotor](/wiki/Kotor "Kotor"). They currently compete in the [Montenegrin Second League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Second_League "Montenegrin Second League").

History
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=OFK_Grbalj&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The first football club in Radanovići, which existed only few seasons, was founded in 1970. After many years, the club was refounded in June 1995[[1]](#cite_note-1) and in their first season the team gained promotion to the [Montenegrin Republic League](/wiki/Montenegrin_clubs_in_Yugoslav_football_competitions_(1946%E2%80%932006)#Montenegrin_Republic_League "Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946–2006)") for the 1996–97 season (third tier of the [FR Yugoslavia](/wiki/FR_Yugoslavia "FR Yugoslavia") football system). After only three seasons in the Republic League, in the summer of 1999, OFK Grbalj (*OFC Humpback*) became a member of the [FR Yugoslavia Second League](/wiki/1999%E2%80%932000_Second_League_of_FR_Yugoslavia "1999–2000 Second League of FR Yugoslavia"), which was the biggest success of the team until 2006.[[2]](#cite_note-2) OFK Grbalj spent four seasons in the Second Yugoslav League.  
After [Montenegrin independence](/wiki/Montenegrin_independence_referendum,_2006 "Montenegrin independence referendum, 2006"), OFK Grbalj became a member of the [Montenegrin First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League "Montenegrin First League"). In the 2006–07 season, the team achieved third place, just behind two of the most successful teams in national competitions, [Zeta](/wiki/FK_Zeta "FK Zeta") and [Budućnost Podgorica](/wiki/FK_Budu%C4%87nost_Podgorica "FK Budućnost Podgorica"). Over the next two seasons, OFK Grbalj finished as a fourth-placed team. During subsequent seasons, the team didn't achieve the same successes as in their first seasons in top-tier competition, but they were never relegated from the First League.  
OFK Grbalj holds two all-time records in the Montenegrin First League. On 29 May 2010 they defeated [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom "FK Kom") 11–0, which is the biggest margin of victory in the history of league. Five years later, on 23 May 2015, OFK Grbalj beat [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar "FK Mornar") in [Bar](/wiki/Bar,_Montenegro "Bar, Montenegro") 7–0, which is the biggest away victory in league.  
In the 2016–17 season, OFK Grbalj had the greatest success in their history by reaching the [Montenegrin Cup final](/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Montenegrin_Cup "2016–17 Montenegrin Cup"). They lost game against [Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 "FK Sutjeska Nikšić") 1–0.  
After 14 consecutive seasons in top-tier, OFK Grbalj finished as a last-placed team in [2019-20 Montenegrin First League](/wiki/2019-20_Montenegrin_First_League "2019-20 Montenegrin First League"). After the campaign full of disappointing results, team from Radanovići was relegated to [Montenegrin Second League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Second_League "Montenegrin Second League").

Stadium
-------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=OFK_Grbalj&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Stadium")]

Main article: [Stadion Donja Sutvara](/wiki/Stadion_Donja_Sutvara "Stadion Donja Sutvara")

OFK Grbalj play at [Stadion Donja Sutvara](/wiki/Stadion_Donja_Sutvara "Stadion Donja Sutvara"), near the main road between [Budva](/wiki/Budva "Budva") and [Kotor](/wiki/Kotor "Kotor"). Stadium capacity is 1,500 seats on one stand and it doesn't meet UEFA standards for European competitions. Except the main ground, there is a smaller artificial pitch at Donja Sutvara football complex.

Anderlecht\") (34 titles) |\\n| Most appearances | [Raymond Mommens](/wiki/Raymond_Mommens \"Raymond Mommens\") (614) |\\n| Top scorer | [Albert De Cleyn](/wiki/Albert_De_Cleyn \"Albert De Cleyn\") (377) |\\n| Broadcaster(s) | [DAZN](/wiki/DAZN \"DAZN\") (2025-2030) |\\n| Website | [proleague.be](https://www.proleague.be/) (in Dutch) |\\n| *Current: [2025–26 Belgian Pro League](/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Belgian_Pro_League \"2025–26 Belgian Pro League\")* | |\\n\\nThe **Belgian Pro League**,[[1]](#cite_note-1) officially the **[Jupiler](/wiki/Jupiler \"Jupiler\") Pro League** (Dutch pronunciation: [[ˈʑypilɛr ˈproː ˌlik]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Dutch \"Help:IPA/Dutch\")) for sponsorship reasons, is a professional [association football](/wiki/Association_football \"Association football\") league in [Belgium](/wiki/Belgium \"Belgium\") and the highest level of the [Belgian football league system](/wiki/Belgian_football_league_system \"Belgian football league system\"). Contested by 16 clubs from the [2023–24 season](/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_Belgian_Pro_League \"2023–24 Belgian Pro League\") until 2025–26 when it will expand to 18 teams from 2026–27 onwards, it operates on a system of [promotion and relegation](/wiki/Promotion_and_relegation \"Promotion and relegation\") with the [Challenger Pro League](/wiki/Challenger_Pro_League \"Challenger Pro League\").\\n\\nSeasons run from late July to late March, with teams playing 30 matches each in the regular season, and then entering **Play-offs I** (also known as the *Championship Playoff*, *title playoffs* or *Champions\\' play-offs*[[2]](#cite_note-Officialranking-2)), **Play-offs II** (also known as the *Europa League playoff* or *Europe play-offs*[[2]](#cite_note-Officialranking-2)) or **Play-offs III** (also known as the *Relegation play-offs*[[2]](#cite_note-Officialranking-2)) according to their position in the regular season. Play-offs I are contested by the top-six clubs in the regular season, with each club playing each other twice. The teams finishing in 15th and 16th place are relegated directly, however, the 14th place team plays a promotion-relegation play-off against the 3rd place team of the Challenger Pro League.\\n\\nThe competition was created in 1895 by the [Royal Belgian Football Association](/wiki/Royal_Belgian_Football_Association \"Royal Belgian Football Association\") and was first won by [FC Liégeois](/wiki/RFC_Li%C3%A8ge \"RFC Liège\"). Of the 78 clubs to have competed in the first division since its creation, 16 have been crowned champions of Belgium. [Anderlecht](/wiki/R.S.C._Anderlecht \"R.S.C. Anderlecht\") is the most successful league club with 34 titles, followed by [Club Brugge](/wiki/Club_Brugge_KV \"Club Brugge KV\") (19), [Union Saint-Gilloise](/wiki/Royale_Union_Saint-Gilloise \"Royale Union Saint-Gilloise\") (12) and [Standard Liège](/wiki/Standard_Li%C3%A8ge \"Standard Liège\") (10). It is currently ranked 8th in the [UEFA rankings](/wiki/UEFA_coefficient \"UEFA coefficient\") of leagues based on performances in European competitions over the last five-years.[[3]](#cite_note-3) The competition was ranked 3rd when the UEFA first published their ranking in 1979 and also the next year in 1980, which is the best ranking the Belgian First Division has ever achieved.\\n\\nHistory\\n-------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: History\")]\\n\\n### Origins (1895–1914)\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=2 \"Edit section: Origins (1895–1914)\")]\\n\\nThe first league in Belgian football was held in [1895–96](/wiki/1895%E2%80%9396_Belgian_First_Division \"1895–96 Belgian First Division\") as a [round-robin tournament](/wiki/Round-robin_tournament \"Round-robin tournament\") with seven teams: [Antwerp FC](/wiki/Royal_Antwerp_F.C. \"Royal Antwerp F.C.\"), [FC Brugeois](/wiki/Club_Brugge \"Club Brugge\"), [FC Liégeois](/wiki/RFC_Li%C3%A8ge \"RFC Liège\"), [RC de Bruxelles](/wiki/K.F.C._Rhodienne-De_Hoek \"K.F.C. Rhodienne-De Hoek\"), [Léopold Club de Bruxelles](/wiki/R._L%C3%A9opold_Uccle_Forestoise \"R. Léopold Uccle Forestoise\"), [SC de Bruxelles](/wiki/S.C._de_Bruxelles \"S.C. de Bruxelles\"), and [Union d\\'Ixelles](/wiki/Union_F.C._d%27Ixelles \"Union F.C. d\\'Ixelles\"). FC Liégeois became the first champion of Belgium. The first eight titles in Belgian football were all won by FC Liégeois or RC de Bruxelles. There was no promotion and relegation system at the time, but the last two finishers (FC Brugeois and Union d\\'Ixelles) withdrew and a new club entered the competition ([Athletic and Running Club de Bruxelles](/wiki/Athletic_and_Running_Club_de_Bruxelles \"Athletic and Running Club de Bruxelles\")). During the [1896–97](/wiki/1896%E2%80%9397_Belgian_First_Division \"1896–97 Belgian First Division\") season, SC de Bruxelles withdrew, so the [1897–98](/wiki/1897%E2%80%9398_Belgian_First_Division \"1897–98 Belgian First Division\") season was played by five clubs. In the seasons [1898–99](/wiki/1898%E2%80%9399_Belgian_First_Division \"1898–99 Belgian First Division\") and [1899–1900](/wiki/1899%E2%80%931900_Belgian_First_Division \"1899–1900 Belgian First Division\"), the football association introduced a new format with two leagues at the top level and a final game in two legs. The format changed back to one league with nine clubs in [1900–01](/wiki/1900%E2%80%9301_Belgian_First_Division \"1900–01 Belgian First Division\"), then again to two leagues from [1901–02](/wiki/1901%E2%80%9302_Belgian_First_Division \"1901–02 Belgian First Division\") to [1903–04](/wiki/1903%E2%80%9304_Belgian_First_Division \"1903–04 Belgian First Division\"), this time with a final round among the top two teams of each league. In [1904–05](/wiki/1904%E2%80%9305_Belgian_First_Division \"1904–05 Belgian First Division\"), the championship was organised with one league of 11 teams. Athletic and Running Club de Bruxelles withdrew during the season and, from the [1906 season](/wiki/1905%E2%80%9306_Belgian_First_Division \"1905–06 Belgian First Division\") on, a system of promotion and relegation was introduced with the winner of the second division replacing the last-placed team of the first division. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nIn [1906–07](/wiki/1906%E2%80%9307_Belgian_First_Division \"1906–07 Belgian First Division\"), [Union Saint-Gilloise](/wiki/Royale_Union_Saint-Gilloise \"Royale Union Saint-Gilloise\") won their fourth consecutive title as RC de Bruxelles had from 1899–1900 to 1902–03. Both clubs claimed the next three titles before [CS Brugeois](/wiki/Cercle_Brugge_K.S.V. \"Cercle Brugge K.S.V.\") won their first title, finishing one point ahead their rival of FC Brugeois. At the end of the 1907–08 season, the number of teams in the first division was increased from 10 to 12 clubs, with Promotion champion [RC de Gand](/wiki/K.R.C._Gent-Zeehaven \"K.R.C. Gent-Zeehaven\") and runner-up [ESC Forest](/wiki/R.E._Sport%27s_Club \"R.E. Sport\\'s Club\") being promoted while no first division was relegated. As [World War I](/wiki/World_War_I \"World War I\") approached, Daring Club de Bruxelles confirmed its status of challenger, even winning the title in [1911–12](/wiki/1911%E2%80%9312_Belgian_First_Division \"1911–12 Belgian First Division\") and [1913–14](/wiki/1913%E2%80%9314_Belgian_First_Division \"1913–14 Belgian First Division\"). Only Union Saint-Gilloise could face them in that period, winning the [1912–13](/wiki/1912%E2%80%9313_Belgian_First_Division \"1912–13 Belgian First Division\") championship with a better goal difference. Since 1911–12, two clubs are relegated each year to the Promotion and two clubs from the Promotion are promoted.[[4]](#cite_note-4)\\n\\n### After World War I (1919–1945)\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=3 \"Edit section: After World War I (1919–1945)\")]\\n\\nDuring World War I, the football championship was suspended. It resumed in [1919–20](/wiki/1919%E2%80%9320_Belgian_First_Division \"1919–20 Belgian First Division\") with FC Brugeois claiming their first title after five second places, among which were two lost final games and one lost test-match. At the end of the [1920–21 season](/wiki/1920%E2%80%9321_Belgian_First_Division \"1920–21 Belgian First Division\"), the number of teams was increased from 12 to 14, with only [Uccle Sport](/wiki/R._Uccle_Sport \"R. Uccle Sport\"), the last-placed team of the first division, being relegated, and the first three teams from the Promotion being promoted ([Standard Club Liégeois](/wiki/Standard_Li%C3%A8ge \"Standard Liège\"), [FC Malinois](/wiki/KV_Mechelen \"KV Mechelen\"), and [RSC Anderlechtois](/wiki/R.S.C._Anderlecht \"R.S.C. Anderlecht\")). From [1921–22](/wiki/1921%E2%80%9322_Belgian_First_Division \"1921–22 Belgian First Division\") to [1931–32](/wiki/1931%E2%80%9332_Belgian_First_Division \"1931–32 Belgian First Division\"), the decade was dominated by teams from the province of [Antwerp](/wiki/Antwerp_(province) \"Antwerp (province)\"): [Beerschot AC](/wiki/Beerschot_AC \"Beerschot AC\"), with [Raymond Braine](/wiki/Raymond_Braine \"Raymond Braine\"), won their first five titles, Antwerp FC their first two and the small club of [Liersche SK](/wiki/Lierse_S.K._(1906) \"Lierse S.K. (1906)\") (led by striker [Bernard Voorhoof](/wiki/Bernard_Voorhoof \"Bernard Voorhoof\")) won their first one in 1931–32. The challengers at the time were CS Brugeois (two titles in that period), Union Saint-Gilloise (one title), Daring Club de Bruxelles and Standard Club Liégeois. Starting 25 December 1932, Union Saint-Gilloise had a record 60 games unbeaten run in the championship (spanning three seasons), winning the [1932–33](/wiki/1932%E2%80%9333_Belgian_First_Division \"1932–33 Belgian First Division\"), [1933–34](/wiki/1933%E2%80%9334_Belgian_First_Division \"1933–34 Belgian First Division\"), and [1934–35](/wiki/1934%E2%80%9335_Belgian_First_Division \"1934–35 Belgian First Division\") titles. The rival of Union during this period was [Daring Club de Bruxelles](/wiki/Daring_Club_de_Bruxelles \"Daring Club de Bruxelles\"). They claimed the next two championships. Following the come-back of player [Raymond Braine](/wiki/Raymond_Braine \"Raymond Braine\") to Beerschot, the [Antwerp](/wiki/Antwerp \"Antwerp\") club won the last two titles before [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II \"World War II\"). [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nOn 10 May 1940, German troops invaded Belgium and the seasons 1939–40 and 1940–41 were suspended. The competition resumed in September 1941 and Liersche SK won their second title. At the end of the season, no club was relegated and the number of clubs was increased from 14 to 16. The [next season](/wiki/1942%E2%80%9343_Belgian_First_Division \"1942–43 Belgian First Division\"), Liersche SK lost three key players (two of them in a bomb attack and the other one due to a heavy injury sustained on the pitch) and they ended at 3rd place while the neighbours of [KV Mechelen](/wiki/KV_Mechelen \"KV Mechelen\") became champion for the first time in their history. In [1943–44](/wiki/1943%E2%80%9344_Belgian_First_Division \"1943–44 Belgian First Division\"), Antwerp FC won the title. The league was suspended again in 1944–45 because of World War II.[[5]](#cite_note-5)\\n\\n### After World War II (1945–1980)\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=4 \"Edit section: After World War II (1945–1980)\")]\\n\\nThe league resumed play in [1945–46](/wiki/1945%E2%80%9346_Belgian_First_Division \"1945–46 Belgian First Division\") with a title for KV Mechelen. At the start of that season, the First Division went from 16 to 19 clubs, with three clubs promoted from the First Division and no team being relegated. The [top scorer](/wiki/Belgian_First_Division_top_scorers \"Belgian First Division top scorers\") award was also introduced that season, won by [Bert De Cleyn](/wiki/Bert_De_Cleyn \"Bert De Cleyn\") from KV Mechelen. Two seasons later, five clubs were relegated and two promoted. In [1946–47](/wiki/1946%E2%80%9347_Belgian_First_Division \"1946–47 Belgian First Division\"), RSC Anderlechtois won their first championship with [Jef Mermans](/wiki/Joseph_Mermans \"Joseph Mermans\") as the key striker and they dominated the Belgian football over the next 9 years with 6 more titles, with KV Mechelen (in [1947–48](/wiki/1947%E2%80%9348_Belgian_First_Division \"1947–48 Belgian First Division\")) and FC Liégeois (in [1951–52](/wiki/1951%E2%80%9352_Belgian_First_Division \"1951–52 Belgian First Division\") and [1952–53](/wiki/1952%E2%80%9353_Belgian_First_Division \"1952–53 Belgian First Division\")) claiming the remaining titles. The [Belgian Golden Shoe](/wiki/Belgian_Golden_Shoe \"Belgian Golden Shoe\") award was introduced in 1954, rewarding the best player in the first division for the past calendar year, thus over two half seasons. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nIn the late 1950s Standard lifted the trophy for the first time in [1957–58](/wiki/1957%E2%80%9358_Belgian_First_Division \"1957–58 Belgian First Division\") and they eventually became one of Anderlecht\\'s biggest rivals in the league (until their 8th title in [1982–83](/wiki/1982%E2%80%9383_Belgian_First_Division \"1982–83 Belgian First Division\")). The other titles in the late 1950s were won by Antwerp FC and Anderlecht. In the 1960s, the Anderlecht team of [Paul Van Himst](/wiki/Paul_Van_Himst \"Paul Van Himst\") claimed six titles (with the Belgian record of five consecutives titles between [1963–64](/wiki/1963%E2%80%9364_Belgian_First_Division \"1963–64 Belgian First Division\") and [1967–68](/wiki/1967%E2%80%9368_Belgian_First_Division \"1967–68 Belgian First Division\")), while Standard claimed three and Lierse one. Standard, with key player [Wilfried Van Moer](/wiki/Wilfried_Van_Moer \"Wilfried Van Moer\"), won the first two titles of the 1970s, which gave them their only treble so far (together with the [1968–69](/wiki/1968%E2%80%9369_Belgian_First_Division \"1968–69 Belgian First Division\") title). [1974–75](/wiki/1974%E2%80%9375_Belgian_First_Division \"1974–75 Belgian First Division\") was the only season with as many as 20 clubs in the league\\'s history. Belgian clubs started to perform well in European Cups in the 1970s, with Anderlecht winning the [1975–76 European Cup Winners\\' Cup](/wiki/1975%E2%80%9376_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup \"1975–76 European Cup Winners\\' Cup\") and Club Brugge losing to [Liverpool F.C.](/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. \"Liverpool F.C.\") in the [1975–76 UEFA Cup](/wiki/1975%E2%80%9376_UEFA_Cup \"1975–76 UEFA Cup\") [final](/wiki/1976_UEFA_Cup_Final \"1976 UEFA Cup Final\"). The following season, Anderlecht lost to [Hamburger SV](/wiki/Hamburger_SV \"Hamburger SV\") in the [Cup Winners\\' Cup](/wiki/1976%E2%80%9377_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup \"1976–77 European Cup Winners\\' Cup\") final and in [1977–78](/wiki/1977%E2%80%9378_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup \"1977–78 European Cup Winners\\' Cup\") won for the second time, while Club Brugge lost the [European Cup](/wiki/1977%E2%80%9378_European_Cup \"1977–78 European Cup\") to Liverpool F.C.. In the Belgian First Division, Club Brugge claimed four titles in the decade, while Anderlecht claimed two and [R White Daring Molenbeek](/wiki/R.W.D._Molenbeek_(1909) \"R.W.D. Molenbeek (1909)\") (the successor of Daring Club de Bruxelles) with [Johan Boskamp](/wiki/Johan_Boskamp \"Johan Boskamp\") and [KSK Beveren](/wiki/K.S.K._Beveren \"K.S.K. Beveren\") with goalkeeper [Jean-Marie Pfaff](/wiki/Jean-Marie_Pfaff \"Jean-Marie Pfaff\") each claimed their first Belgian championship. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\n### Recent years (1980–present)\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=5 \"Edit section: Recent years (1980–present)\")]\\n\\nIn the 1980s, the European successes continued for Belgian clubs with Standard reaching the [1981–82 European Cup Winners\\' Cup](/wiki/1981%E2%80%9382_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup \"1981–82 European Cup Winners\\' Cup\") final, Anderlecht winning the [1982–83 UEFA Cup](/wiki/1982%E2%80%9383_UEFA_Cup \"1982–83 UEFA Cup\") and losing the [next UEFA Cup](/wiki/1983%E2%80%9384_UEFA_Cup \"1983–84 UEFA Cup\") final and KV Mechelen winning the [1987–88 European Cup Winners\\' Cup](/wiki/1987%E2%80%9388_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup \"1987–88 European Cup Winners\\' Cup\"). In the domestic league, Anderlecht won their 20th title in [1986–87](/wiki/1986%E2%80%9387_Belgian_First_Division \"1986–87 Belgian First Division\"), which was also the 4th of the decade. Club Brugge and Standard each won two titles in the 1980s and KSK Beveren and KV Mechelen one each. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nIn the 1990s, Belgium\\'s teams performances were diminished in European competitions, with only RSC Anderlecht and Royal Antwerp FC reaching the [European Cup Winners\\' Cup](/wiki/European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup \"European Cup Winners\\' Cup\") final, respectively in [1989–90](/wiki/1989%E2%80%9390_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup \"1989–90 European Cup Winners\\' Cup\") and in [1992–93](/wiki/1992%E2%80%9393_European_Cup_Winners%27_Cup \"1992–93 European Cup Winners\\' Cup\"). In the home league, RSC Anderlecht took four titles during the decade, while Club Brugge cemented their status as main contender with four titles. The remaining two titles went to Lierse SK and newcomer [Racing Genk](/wiki/K.R.C._Genk \"K.R.C. Genk\"). The 2000s brought a bright European start, with Anderlecht reaching the second group stage in the [2000–01 UEFA Champions League](/wiki/2000%E2%80%9301_UEFA_Champions_League \"2000–01 UEFA Champions League\"), but the rest of the decade Belgian clubs were again not very successful in European competitions. In the league, RSC Anderlecht won five titles in the decade, with Club Brugge claiming two titles and Racing Genk taking their second title. At the end of the decade, [Standard Liège](/wiki/Standard_Li%C3%A8ge \"Standard Liège\") returned as a title contender with two consecutive titles, 25 years after their [1982–83](/wiki/1982%E2%80%9383_Belgian_First_Division \"1982–83 Belgian First Division\") title. At the end of the 2000s, the highest level in Belgian football was reshaped, with a play-off round after the regular season. RSC Anderlecht won the [first championship in this new format](/wiki/Belgian_Pro_League_2009-10 \"Belgian Pro League 2009-10\"), which was their 30th title. [*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] After another two titles for Anderlecht, [KAA Gent](/wiki/KAA_Gent \"KAA Gent\") was the surprise winner of the Championship in 2015. The following seven years, Club Brugge would win the league five times. Anderlecht and Genk won the title on the other occasions. [Union Saint-Gilloise](/wiki/Royale_Union_Saint-Gilloise \"Royale Union Saint-Gilloise\") came close to shocking the footballing world by almost winning the league in [2021–22](/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Belgian_First_Division_A \"2021–22 Belgian First Division A\"). In their first season at the top flight in 48 years, they started the play-offs in first place, but came just short of denying Club Brugge their third consecutive title.[[6]](#cite_note-6)\\n\\nCompetition format and naming\\n-----------------------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=6 \"Edit section: Competition format and naming\")]\\n\\nThe competition format has undergone several changes since 2009, but the most significant one was the introduction of playoffs after completion of the regular season from the 2009–10 season. At that time the number of teams also decreased from 18 to 16 and there was the introduction of matches being played during the [Christmas holidays](/wiki/Christmas \"Christmas\"). The change was initially met with criticism, with many at that time pointing out that the Dutch [Eredivisie](/wiki/Eredivisie \"Eredivisie\") has already abandoned playoffs after three seasons. Anderlecht won the first championship in this new format, the [Belgian Pro League 2009-10](/wiki/Belgian_Pro_League_2009-10 \"Belgian Pro League 2009-10\"), which was their 30th Belgian championship.\\n\\nFollowing the 2015–16 season, the number of professional teams in Belgium was brought down to 24, which mostly affected the teams playing at the second level of the Belgian football pyramid as the [Belgian Second Division](/wiki/Belgian_Second_Division \"Belgian Second Division\") was replaced by the [Belgian First Division B](/wiki/Belgian_First_Division_B \"Belgian First Division B\") and the number of teams dropped to eight.\\n\\nDue to the redesign of the UEFA competitions and the extra burden on the football season calendar (4 extra matchdays for clubs in Europe), there was a need to reduce the number of matches in the Belgian League. Despite the playoff format being very successful with added excitement and decisions often at the very end of the season, the clubs could not agree on a format with fewer teams or altered playoffs and hence it was decided end of February 2025 to return to a system without playoffs from the 2026–27 season onwards, while expanding the top division from 16 to 18 teams.\\n\\nMatches are usually played on Saturdays at 20.00; however, some matchdays are played on Wednesdays. Furthermore, in recent years, some games are played on Fridays or during the weekend at different times (e.g., Saturday at 18.00 or Sunday at 13.00 or 20.00), as decided by the owner of television rights. Each team playing the Pro League must have been granted the Belgian professional football license guaranteeing the club has no excessive debts, has a secure stadium, etc. This was introduced in the 2001–02 season to decrease the number of teams in the division and ensure a higher level of professionalism in the clubs playing in the top flight of Belgian football. Originally, clubs that could not get the license were supposed not to be replaced (and sent to the [third division](/wiki/Belgian_Third_Division \"Belgian Third Division\")). However, it is still not effective as, for example, [KSK Beveren](/wiki/K.S.K._Beveren \"K.S.K. Beveren\") finished 18th (last) in 2001–2002, but was saved as [KSC Eendracht Aalst](/wiki/K.S.C._Eendracht_Aalst \"K.S.C. Eendracht Aalst\") (17th) and [RWD Molenbeek](/wiki/R.W.D._Molenbeek_(1909) \"R.W.D. Molenbeek (1909)\") (10th) were refused their license.\\n\\n### Regular season\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=7 \"Edit section: Regular season\")]\\n\\nEach of the 16 competitors in the Pro League plays every other team twice in the regular season, for a total of 30 matches between August and April. A win earns three points and a draw earns one point. Teams are ranked by total points, then by total wins and finally by goal difference, number of scored goals, number of away goals, and number of away wins. If teams are still level, a test-match is played in two legs to determine the final order in the standings. A playoff phase is then played from May.\\n\\n### Championship Play-off\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=8 \"Edit section: Championship Play-off\")]\\n\\nThe point system in the championship playoff is the same as during the regular season, except that each team starts with half of the points they won in the regular season, rounded up to the nearest integer. The points gained by rounding are deducted in the case of a tie.\\n\\nThe top six teams from the regular season enter the championship playoff, with the first-placed team winning the championship of Belgium. Zulte Waregem\") | 6th | • | | 2nd | 4th | • | 6th | | • | | • | | | × | |  |\\n\\n### Europa League Playoff\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=11 \"Edit section: Europa League Playoff\")]\\n\\nUntil 2016, the teams ranked 7 to 14 after the regular season enter the playoffs 2, with teams ranked 7th, 9th, 12th, and 14th entering group A and teams ranked 8th, 10th, 11th, and 13th entering group B. In each group, each team plays each of its three opponents twice. The winner of each group played the final game in two legs to determine the winner of the playoffs 2. The winner of the playoffs 2 then plays a home and away game against either the fourth-place or fifth-place team from the playoffs 1 for the final Europa League ticket, with the opponent depending on whether the Belgian Cup winner ended in the top four of the playoff 1 or not.\\n\\nFrom 2016, the system was changed as now the teams ranked 7 to 16 are joined by six teams from the [Belgian First Division B](/wiki/Belgian_First_Division_B \"Belgian First Division B\") and divided into four groups of four teams. The winners of each groups now play a single match to determine the overall playoff winner, with the winner playing the fifth-placed team from playoff 1 in a single match for the final Europa League ticket.\\n\\n### Relegation playoff\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=12 \"Edit section: Relegation playoff\")]\\n\\nUntil 2015, a relegation playoff was played between the teams ranked 15th and 16th after the regular season. It consisted of five games between the two teams. The 15th-placed team started the playoffs with three points whereas the 16th-placed team started from zero. The loser of the relegation playoff was relegated to the second division. The winner of that playoff had to enter the [Belgian Second Division final round](/wiki/Belgian_Second_Division_final_round \"Belgian Second Division final round\") with three teams from the second division. The winner of this Final Round played in the First Division the season thereafter.\\n\\nFrom 2015 to 2023, the relegation playoff ceased to exist, as now the 16th-place team relegates directly, whereas the 15th placed team takes part in the Europa League playoff. The [2015–16 Belgian Pro League](/wiki/2015%E2%80%9316_Belgian_Pro_League \"2015–16 Belgian Pro League\") was an exception as during that season the 15th placed team did not take part in any playoff, with the season for that team ending after the regular season.\\n\\nFrom 2023 onwards, the relegation play-off was played between the teams ranked 13th and 16th after the regular season. After the relegation play-off battle, two teams are relegated directly to the Challenger Pro League and one team will play against 3rd place of Challenger Pro League due to avoid relegation.\\n\\n### Qualification for European competitions\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=13 \"Edit section: Qualification for European competitions\")]\\n\\nFor the 2010–11 season, the Belgian champion and the runner-up qualify for the 3rd [UEFA Champions League](/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League \"UEFA Champions League\") qualifying round (of 4).[[7]](#cite_note-7) The [Belgian Cup](/wiki/Belgian_Cup \"Belgian Cup\") winner (or the Cup finalist if the Cup winner finished first or second in the league) qualifies for the play-off of the [UEFA Europa League](/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League \"UEFA Europa League\"). The third-placed team (or the fourth-placed team if the Cup winner finished third in the league) qualifies for the 3rd and last qualifying round and the winner of the game between the play-offs 2 winner and the fourth-placed team (or the fifth-placed team if the Cup winner finished fourth) qualifies for the 2nd qualifying round.[[8]](#cite_note-8)\\n\\n### Naming\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=14 \"Edit section: Naming\")]\\n\\n* 1895–1904: Championship Cup\\n* 1904–1926: First Division\\n* 1926–1952: Division of Honour\\n* 1952–2016: First Division\\n* 2016–2022: First Division A\\n* 2022–present: Belgian Pro League\\n\\nMedia coverage\\n--------------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=15 \"Edit section: Media coverage\")]\\n\\nThe Belgian Football Association sells the television rights for the Belgian First Division every three years. In 2005, the newly created Belgian TV channel [Proximus TV](/wiki/Proximus_TV \"Proximus TV\") bought the TV rights for a record amount of €36 million per season until 2019–20.\\n\\nIn May 2008, the rights were again sold to Belgacom TV in association with both public broadcasters [VRT](/wiki/Vlaamse_Radio-_en_Televisieomroep \"Vlaamse Radio- en Televisieomroep\") (Dutch) and [RTBF](/wiki/RTBF \"RTBF\") (French) for an amount of €45.7 million per season.[[9]](#cite_note-9) RTBF and VRT thus received the rights to show summaries of first division games, as well as rights to a weekly magazine on the competition. Belgacom TV received the rights to show each game in the competition.\\n\\nOn 12 June 2020 Aser\\'s [Eleven Sports](/wiki/Eleven_Sports \"Eleven Sports\") and the Pro League reached an agreement on the new domestic and international media contract for the coming five years. As exclusive global rights holder, Eleven Sports will air the rights of all Pro League competitions for the next five seasons from 2020–21 until 2024–25, with both public broadcasters Play 4 (Dutch) and RTBF (French) lands the rights for highlights again.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)\\n\\nClubs\\n-----\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=16 \"Edit section: Clubs\")]\\n\\n### Champions\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=17 \"Edit section: Champions\")]\\n\\nMain article: [List of Belgian football champions](/wiki/List_of_Belgian_football_champions \"List of Belgian football champions\")\\n\\n| Club | Number Of Championships | Number Of Runner-ups | Years Of Championships |\\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\\n| **[RSC Anderlecht](/wiki/R.S.C._Anderlecht \"R.S.C. The first club to start a game with 11 foreign players was [KSC Lokeren](/wiki/K.S.C._Lokeren_Oost-Vlaanderen \"K.S.C. Lokeren Oost-Vlaanderen\") in 2001. Every year, players are elected for [Belgian Golden Shoe](/wiki/Belgian_Golden_Shoe \"Belgian Golden Shoe\") awards, the highest awards a player can receive in Belgian competitions, but also for [Belgian professional football awards](/wiki/Belgian_professional_football_awards \"Belgian professional football awards\"). Players with African descent, origin or nationality can claim a [Belgian Ebony Shoe](/wiki/Belgian_Ebony_Shoe \"Belgian Ebony Shoe\") award. Players compete also every season for the Belgian First Division top scorer, since the 1945–46 season.\\n\\n### Top scorers\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit&section=22 \"Edit section: Top scorers\")]\\n\\nAll-time top scorers in the Belgian First Division\\n\\n| Rank | Player | Goals |\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| 1 | [Albert De Cleyn](/wiki/Albert_De_Cleyn \"Albert De Cleyn\") | 377 |\\n| 2 | [Joseph Mermans](/wiki/Joseph_Mermans \"Joseph Mermans\") | 339 |\\n| 3 | [Bernard Voorhoof](/wiki/Bernard_Voorhoof \"Bernard Voorhoof\") | 281 |\\n| 4 | [Arthur Ceuleers](/wiki/Arthur_Ceuleers \"Arthur Ceuleers\") | 280 |\\n| 5 | [Rik Coppens](/wiki/Rik_Coppens \"Rik Coppens\") | 258 |\\n| 6 | [Erwin Vandenbergh](/wiki/Erwin_Vandenbergh \"Erwin Vandenbergh\") | 252 |\\n| 7 | [Paul Van Himst](/wiki/Paul_Van_Himst \"Paul Van Himst\") | 237 |\\n| 8 | [Jan Ceulemans](/wiki/Jan_Ceulemans \"Jan Ceulemans\") | 230 |\\n| As of 16\\xa0July\\xa02000[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Belgian_Pro_League&action=edit)[[14]](#cite_note-14) | | |\\n\\nMain article: [Belgian First Division A top scorers](/wiki/Belgian_First_Division_A_top_scorers \"Belgian First Division A top scorers\")\\n\\n[Erwin Vandenbergh](/wiki/Erwin_Vandenbergh \"Erwin Vandenbergh\") is the only player to have claimed the top scorer title four consecutive times, between 1979–80 and 1982–83 (the first three times while at [Lierse SK](/wiki/Lierse_S.K._(1906) \"Lierse S.K. (1906)\") and the last time while at [RSC Anderlecht](/wiki/R.S.C._Anderlecht \"R.S.C. Anderlecht\")). He is also the player to have claimed the most Belgian First Division top scorer titles in his career (six times with three different clubs: three times with Lierse SK, twice with RSC Anderlecht and once with [KAA Gent](/wiki/K.A.A._Gent \"K.A.A. Gent\")). [Victor Wegria](/wiki/Victor_Wegria \"Victor Wegria\") and [Josip Weber](/wiki/Josip_Weber \"Josip Weber\") won the title three consecutive times (resp. between 1958–59 and 1960–61 while at [RFC Liégeois](/wiki/RFC_Li%C3%A8ge \"RFC Liège\") and between 1991–92 and 1993–94 while at [Cercle Brugge KSV](/wiki/Cercle_Brugge_K.S.V. \"Cercle Brugge K.S.V.\")). Wegria eventually finished top scorer a 4th time in 1962–63 still with RFC Liégeois, making him the second player with the most top scorer titles in the history of Belgian First Division top scorers.\\n\\nThe introduction of this title of honour in 1945 was maybe a little too late for first winner [Albert De Cleyn](/wiki/Albert_De_Cleyn \"Albert De Cleyn\") as this player has scored the most goals in the history of the Belgian First Division since 1895 (350 goals in 395 games between 1932 and 1954 with [KV Mechelen](/wiki/Y.R._K.V._Mechelen \"Y.R. K.V. Mechelen\")), though he won the top scorer title only once. Other players in the top ten of the all-time top scorer ranking in the Belgian First Division include [Joseph Mermans](/wiki/Joseph_Mermans \"Joseph Mermans\") (three times top scorer, 339 goals overall in 382 games with RSC Anderlecht), [Bernard Voorhoof](/wiki/Bernard_Voorhoof \"Bernard Voorhoof\") ([Belgium national football team](/wiki/Belgium_national_football_team \"Belgium national football team\") top scorer, 281 goals in 473 matches with Lierse SK), [Rik Coppens](/wiki/Rik_Coppens \"Rik Coppens\") (three times top scorer), Erwin Vandenbergh and [Paul Van Himst](/wiki/Paul_Van_Himst \"Paul Van Himst\") (Belgium top scorer with Bernard Voorhoof, three times top scorer).\\n\\nThe first foreign player to claim the title was Dutchman [Jan Mulder](/wiki/Jan_Mulder_(footballer) \"Jan Mulder (footballer)\") in 1966–67 with RSC Anderlecht. Since then, 25 foreign players have finished top scorer. Only three foreign players claimed the trophy more than once: [Josip Weber](/wiki/Josip_Weber \"Josip Weber\") (twice as a Croat and once as a Belgian), Austrian [Alfred Riedl](/wiki/Alfred_Riedl \"Alfred Riedl\") and most recently Frenchman [Jérémy Perbet](/wiki/J%C3%A9r%C3%A9my_Perbet \"Jérémy Perbet\").\\n\\nInternational results by Belgian \"Serbian Cyrillic alphabet\"): Омладински фудбалски клуб Грбаљ, Serbo-Croatian pronunciation: [[gr̩̂baʎ]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian \"Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian\")) is a [Montenegrin](/wiki/Montenegro \"Montenegro\") professional [football](/wiki/Association_football \"Association football\") club based in the small town of [Radanovići](/wiki/Radanovi%C4%87i,_Kotor \"Radanovići, Kotor\"), municipality of [Kotor](/wiki/Kotor \"Kotor\"). They currently compete in the [Montenegrin Second League](/wiki/Montenegrin_Second_League \"Montenegrin Second League\").\\n\\nHistory\\n-------\\n\\n[[edit](/w/index.php?title=OFK_Grbalj&action=edit&section=1 \"Edit section: History\")]\\n\\nThe first football club in Radanovići, which existed only few seasons, was founded in 1970. After many years, the club was refounded in June 1995[[1]](#cite_note-1) and in their first season the team gained promotion to the [Montenegrin Republic League](/wiki/Montenegrin_clubs_in_Yugoslav_football_competitions_(1946%E2%80%932006)#Montenegrin_Republic_League \"Montenegrin clubs in Yugoslav football competitions (1946–2006)\") for the 1996–97 season (third tier of the [FR Yugoslavia](/wiki/FR_Yugoslavia \"FR Yugoslavia\") football system). After only three seasons in the Republic League, in the summer of 1999, OFK Grbalj (*OFC Humpback*) became a member of the [FR Yugoslavia Second League](/wiki/1999%E2%80%932000_Second_League_of_FR_Yugoslavia \"1999–2000 Second League of FR Yugoslavia\"), which was the biggest success of the team until 2006.[[2]](#cite_note-2) OFK Grbalj spent four seasons in the Second Yugoslav League.  \\nAfter [Montenegrin independence](/wiki/Montenegrin_independence_referendum,_2006 \"Montenegrin independence referendum, 2006\"), OFK Grbalj became a member of the [Montenegrin First League](/wiki/Montenegrin_First_League \"Montenegrin First League\"). In the 2006–07 season, the team achieved third place, just behind two of the most successful teams in national competitions, [Zeta](/wiki/FK_Zeta \"FK Zeta\") and [Budućnost Podgorica](/wiki/FK_Budu%C4%87nost_Podgorica \"FK Budućnost Podgorica\"). Over the next two seasons, OFK Grbalj finished as a fourth-placed team. During subsequent seasons, the team didn\\'t achieve the same successes as in their first seasons in top-tier competition, but they were never relegated from the First League.  \\nOFK Grbalj holds two all-time records in the Montenegrin First League. On 29 May 2010 they defeated [Kom](/wiki/FK_Kom \"FK Kom\") 11–0, which is the biggest margin of victory in the history of league. Five years later, on 23 May 2015, OFK Grbalj beat [Mornar](/wiki/FK_Mornar \"FK Mornar\") in [Bar](/wiki/Bar,_Montenegro \"Bar, Montenegro\") 7–0, which is the biggest away victory in league.  \\nIn the 2016–17 season, OFK Grbalj had the greatest success in their history by reaching the [Montenegrin Cup final](/wiki/2016%E2%80%9317_Montenegrin_Cup \"2016–17 Montenegrin Cup\"). They lost game against [Sutjeska](/wiki/FK_Sutjeska_Nik%C5%A1i%C4%87 \"FK Sutjeska Nikšić\") 1–0.  \\nAfter 14 consecutive seasons in top-tier, OFK Grbalj finished as a last-placed team in [2019-20 Montenegrin First League](/wiki/2019-20_Montenegrin_First_League \"2019-20 Montenegrin First League\").
